questions.question: Define a physical property. Explain, using melting points, why cooking pots are made of iron or aluminium and why solder is used to join electrical wires.
questions.expected_answer: A physical property is a feature of a material that can be observed or measured without changing it into a new substance. Iron (about 1 538 degrees Celsius) and aluminium (about 660 degrees Celsius) have melting points far above the temperature of a stove or fire, so pots do not melt. Solder has a low melting point, so it melts easily under a soldering iron and then sets to hold wires together.

questions.question: Describe how you would test whether a material is an electrical conductor, and explain how both conductors and insulators are used in an electrical cable and a saucepan.
questions.expected_answer: Make a circuit with a cell, a light bulb and wires with a gap; place the material across the gap. If the bulb lights, the material is a conductor; if not, it is an insulator. Cable: copper wires (conductor) carry current; plastic coating (insulator) prevents shocks and short circuits. Saucepan: metal body (good heat conductor) carries heat to the food; plastic or wooden handle (heat insulator) protects the hand.

questions.question: Explain the difference between hardness and strength, define density, and explain why aircraft are built mainly of aluminium alloys.
questions.expected_answer: Hardness is resistance to scratching or denting; strength is the ability to carry a load without breaking. Glass is hard but brittle and breaks easily, so hard does not mean strong. Density is the mass of a material per unit volume (how heavy it is for its size). Aluminium alloys are much less dense than steel (about 2,8 compared with 8 grams per cubic centimetre) yet strong enough, so the aircraft is lighter for its strength, uses less fuel and can carry more.
